title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarks and Runbooks
author: Riley Patel
content:
Overview
--------
This document consolidates our serving runtime reference material: architecture, kernel scheduling heuristics, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, known issues, release highlights, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers who operate or extend the Redwood serving runtime and for on-call responders.

Goals and scope
- Primary goals: predictable latency, high throughput, cost efficiency, and graceful degradation across hosted/dedicated/private deployments.
- Scope: runtime core, scheduler, kernel selection, batching, KV-cache, quantization runtime hooks, profiling tooling, benchmarks, and operational runbooks.

Ownership and contacts
- Primary owner_team: engineering (serving-runtime subteam)
- On-call rotation: serving-runtime-sre (pager duty alias: @redwood-serving-runtime-sre)
- Primary engineers: Riley Patel (author), Jordan Lee (reviewer), Priya Nair (perf lead)

1) Runtime architecture (executive summary)
-----------------------------------------
Short description: a GPU-optimized inference engine that exposes a consistent request API, a scheduling layer that maps requests to execution lanes, and a kernel selection/compilation layer that chooses optimized code paths per model and hardware.

Key components:
- Frontend API (service: runtime-frontend): HTTP/gRPC ingress, auth, request normalization, rate limits.
- Router & policy engine (service: runtime-router): routes by latency policy, cost tier, and region. Implements fallback policies for model variants.
- Scheduler (service: runtime-scheduler): continuous batching, priority lanes, and preemption hooks.
- Execution engine (service: runtime-exec): kernel selection, KV cache management, quantized operators, and memory allocator.
- Observability (service: runtime-metrics): token-level tracing, per-request traces, and end-to-end histograms.
- Cache & storage: KV-cache (in-memory on GPU), model artifacts (S3-like object store), and checkpoint store.

Service-level objectives (examples)
- 99th percentile decode latency (per-token) for seq<=512: <= 45ms for hosted standard tier.
- P95 request latency (end-to-end) for text-completion (seq<=512): <= 120ms.
- Availability SLO for serving-runtime control plane: 99.9% monthly.

2) Kernel scheduling & heuristics
--------------------------------
Principles
- Minimize tail latency by keeping hot-path kernels on optimized lanes.
- Maximize GPU utilization using continuous batching while enforcing per-request latency SLOs.
- Prefer fused kernels for medium-length sequences, fallback to generic kernels for outliers.

Scheduling lanes and priorities
- Lanes:
  - interactive-low-latency (highest priority) — small sequences, short time budgets.
  - standard (default) — balanced throughput/latency.
  - batch-high-throughput — large sequence and batch workloads (bulk inference).
- Preemption policy:
  - interactive lanes can preempt standard lane batches if predicted remaining time > 3x latency SLO.
  - Preemption uses safe checkpoint/resume when possible; otherwise, evict KV cache entries for the evicted slice.

Kernel selection rules (simplified)
1. Check model quantization profile -> use quantized kernels when model flags indicate int8/4 support.
2. If sequence length <= 128 and batch size <= 4 -> use fused attention + rotary kernel variant A.
3. For seq 129-512 -> use tiled attention kernel variant B with progressive KV flush policy.
4. For seq > 512 -> use generic fallback kernel optimized for memory locality.

Config table (example values)
- max_batch_size: \"64\"
- interactive_latency_budget_ms: \"80\"
- kv_cache_size_limit_mb_per_gpu: \"12000\"
- preemption_threshold_ratio: \"3.0\"
- fused_kernel_preference: \"true\"

3) Profiling playbook (runbook + tooling)
-----------------------------------------
When to profile
- New model onboarding, quantization changes, unexpected latency regressions, or hardware changes (driver/runtime updates).

Tools and artifacts
- perf-trace (internal wrapper around nvprof / Nsight / CUPTI)
- trace-collector (aggregates per-request traces into zip archives)
- flamegraph-generator (from perf traces)
- kernel-metrics-exporter (exports per-kernel durations to prometheus)

Standard profiling procedure
1. Reproduce a representative workload in staging (use load-generator: loadgen/runtime-workload).
2. Enable trace sampling at 5% to reduce overhead: runtime-config: trace.sample_rate=0.05.
3. Run perf-trace with --capture-kernel-metrics --capture-kv-ops. Example:

  ./perf-trace --target runtime-exec:gpu0 --duration 120 --capture-kernel-metrics --out profile-2028-09-01.tar.gz

4. Generate flamegraphs: flamegraph-generator profile-2028-09-01.tar.gz --output flame-2028-09-01.svg
5. Correlate kernel durations with request-level histograms and token-level traces. Look for kernels with high variance and long tail.

Profiling checklist
- Verify model quantization flags.
- Confirm appropriate kernel selection was attempted (check runtime-exec logs).
- Capture GPU memory utilization and PCIe transfer rates.
- Capture per-kernel occupancy and SM utilization.

4) Benchmarking suite (how we measure and certify models)
--------------------------------------------------------
Benchmark goals
- Provide reproducible throughput and latency numbers across hardware families (A100, H100, GA100, L40).
- Evaluate impact of batching, quantization, and sequence length distributions.

Benchmark harness components
- loadgen/runtime-bench: configurable request distributions (chat, completion, embeddings, rerank).
- bench-orchestrator: runs experiments across hardware clouds, pins model version and runtime flags, stores results in bench-db.
- bench-dashboard: visualization and historical comparisons.

Canonical benchmark matrix (selected)
- Models: small-7B, medium-13B, large-70B (float16 and int8 variants)
- Hardware: A100-80GB, H100-80GB, L40-48GB
- Sequences: 32, 128, 512, 1024
- Metrics: tokens/sec (throughput), p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU utilization, cost-per-1M-tokens estimate

Example CLI to run a single experiment
  bench-orchestrator run --model small-7B --hw A100 --seq 128 --bs 8 --quant int8 --duration 600 --tags \"canary-2028-09\"

Result interpretation guidance
- Compare p99 / p95 latency to SLOs. If p99 > SLO * 1.5, mark as regression and create an issue with tags: perf/regression.
- Verify tokens/sec vs historical baseline; <90% of baseline triggers triage.

5) Release notes (recent highlights)
-----------------------------------
Release: runtime v3.8.0 (2028-09-10)
- Kernel improvements: merged fused attention v2 for short sequences (reduces p99 per-token latency by ~22%).
- Scheduler: added adaptive preemption threshold to reduce tail latency during bursty traffic.
- Profiling: integrated cupy-based low-overhead counters; perf-trace sampling overhead reduced from 12% to 4%.
- Fixes: memory leak in kv-cache eviction during preemption; fixed incorrect occupancy calculation on H100.

6) Known issues (operational, with workarounds)
---------------------------------------------
- Issue: intermittent p99 spikes on H100 after driver 555.x update (INC-2028-1142).
  - Symptom: p99 latency increases by 2-3x for 30-90s windows.
  - Workaround: roll back to driver 545.x; set runtime-exec env VAR NV_DRIVER_WORKAROUND=true.
  - Permanent fix: scheduled; kernel vendor patch in testing.

- Issue: KV cache stale entries after canary rollouts when model shard mapping changes (INC-2028-1103).
  - Symptom: increased first-token latency for affected requests.
  - Workaround: flush kv-cache on rollout or use canary with cache-isolated nodes.

- Issue: quantized kernels sometimes choose suboptimal tiling for seq ~200 (BUG-2028-089).
  - Symptom: throughput regression on medium-length chat workloads.
  - Mitigation: force fused_kernel_preference=false for affected model; queue fix in PR #5129.

7) Runtime runbooks (for on-call)
--------------------------------
P1: High tail latency (p99 end-to-end > 2x SLO)
1. Check recent deploys: runtime-exec/runtime-scheduler/runtime-router. Roll back last deploy if correlated.
2. Query metrics (prometheus): token_latency_p99, kernel_duration_p99, gpu_utilization.
3. Pull flamegraphs for the window (use trace-collector).
4. If kernel_duration_p99 is elevated -> run perf-trace snapshot.
5. If GPU saturation detected (util > 95% sustained) -> move traffic to spare pool or scale up dedicated nodes.
6. Temporary mitigation: lower batch target on runtime-scheduler: curl -XPOST $ADMIN /v1/runtime/config -d '{"max_batch_size":32}'

P2: Node OOM or GPU OOM
1. Identify affected node via metrics and node exporter logs.
2. Drain node: runtime-admin drain-node <node-id>.
3. If OOM triggered during rollout, revert rollout and trigger kv-cache flush.
4. Collect crashlogs: /var/log/runtime-exec/crash-<timestamp>.tar.gz and attach to incident.

P3: Model quality regression triggered by optimization
1. Validate model outputs using evaluation harness (applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness).
2. If regression is due to quantization, revert to float16 profile and re-run bench matrix.

9) Appendices
------------
A. Example runtime-config (YAML)
  runtime_config:
    max_batch_size: 64
    interactive_latency_budget_ms: 80
    kv_cache_size_limit_mb_per_gpu: 12000
    trace:
      sample_rate: 0.05

B. Useful queries (Prometheus)
- p99 token latency: "histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(token_processing_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))"
- per-kernel p95: "sum(rate(kernel_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (kernel_name, le)"

C. Troubleshooting artifacts to attach to incidents
- profile tarball (perf-trace output), flamegraph svg, runtime-exec logs (last 2000 lines), stack traces, bench DB snapshot id.
